eyebrow: AI Engineering Leadership & Architecture · Chapter Four
subtitle: Lesson 16 · Incident Ownership

eyebrow: "Blameless" does not mean "no one made a mistake"
code:
Goal: understand the SYSTEMIC reasons a mistake
      reached production -- not assign individual fault.

A culture that punishes the mistake teaches people
to hide mistakes -- and near-misses are your best
early-warning signal.
caption: A blameless postmortem is honest about what happened, not about who to blame.

eyebrow: The incident: a bad deploy at Northbeam
code:
Northbeam's support assistant returned errors for
~12% of requests for 40 minutes before rollback.

Surface explanation: "a bad deploy."
True -- but not a root cause. It doesn't explain WHY
the deploy was bad, or why nothing caught it first.
caption: A true explanation and a root cause are not the same thing.

eyebrow: The 5 Whys: pushing past the surface
code:
Why did it fail?        -> Bug handling one vector-DB response format.
Why wasn't it caught?   -> Tests didn't cover that format.
Why didn't tests cover it? -> Rare in test data, common in one real
                              document category.
Why wasn't that category in test data? -> Test data sampled months
                              before that category existed.
Why wasn't it kept in sync? -> No process re-samples test data,
                              ever.
caption: Five steps down, the real root cause is a process gap -- not a careless engineer.

eyebrow: The real deliverable: action items, not the narrative
code:
"Someone should look into test data coverage
 eventually."                     -- not an action item

"Priya will build an automated monthly test-data
 resampling job by end of next sprint."   -- an action item
caption: A postmortem is only as useful as the gap it actually closes.
